gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Anker SOLIX S2000's solar port takes only 8.2 A below 28 V (about 230 W at most from 12 V-class panels), so its 400 W needs a 28-60 V panel such as one Anker PS400 or two PS200 in parallel, and that Anker's own table marks it 'Expandable Battery: No' and '12V DC Port: No'.
standout_why: I opened only one rival page, Powerbencher (cited). It already says the S2000 has no 12 V DC output and that solar input caps at 400 W; it says nothing on the S2000's solar voltage/current window, which panels reach 400 W, or expansion. It also says 'No solar input figure is published' and 'No expansion battery is listed' for the Jackery Explorer 2000 v2. The cited Jackery product page returned HTTP 429 on every try, so I could not compare against it. I did not open solargenreview, keptpowered, thiswatt, slopsheets, powerstations.reviews, offgridbenchmark or smartgadgetkit.
decides: It confirms the S2000 as the lightest row at 35.7 lb but does not move the weight ranking. It adds three limits a buyer should see before paying: no expansion battery, no 12 V socket, and 400 W of solar only from a 28-60 V panel. Separately, Anker's US page read today says S2000 orders placed on or after Nov. 26 ship within 7-13 weeks. Under the page's four-week rule that stops it being the pick if another row ships sooner, so the Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 (39.5 lb per ChatGPT's results; its page was unreadable today) needs its stock and price read before the pick is set.

findings.label: Solar (MPPT) input window, XT60i port
findings.value: 8.2 A max below 28 V; a higher current limit from 28 V to 60 V; 400 W max
findings.source_title: Anker SOLIX S2000 (Anker SOLIX Canada product page, spec table)
findings.note: This is Anker's Canadian page; the US page gives no solar voltage or current. The fetch returned the line as '1V - 28V⎓8.2A; 28V - 60V⎓2.5A Max (400W Max)'. Leading digits look dropped: 2.5 A at 60 V is only 150 W, and 400 W / 12.5 A = 32 V fits. The likely true line is '11V - 28V⎓8.2A; 28V - 60V⎓12.5A', which a search snippet of Anker's support article also showed, but that article would not open. Re-read in a browser before printing 11 V or 12.5 A. The '28V⎓8.2A' and '400W Max' parts read cleanly.

findings.label: Most solar it can take from a panel array under 28 V
findings.source_title: Anker SOLIX S2000 (Anker SOLIX Canada product page, spec table)
findings.note: Arithmetic on Anker's figures: 28 V × 8.2 A = 229.6 W. Paralleled 12 V-class panels sit below 28 V, so they cannot reach the 400 W cap however many are added.

findings.label: Anker panels that reach the 400 W input
findings.value: One PS400 (48 V / 8.33 A) or two PS200 (48 V / 4.16 A each); input capped at 400 W even with a larger array
findings.source_title: Solar panel sizing calculator for a 2000Wh power station (Anker SOLIX blog, dated 02/09/2026)
findings.note: Anker's words: 'use one PS400 or two compatible PS200 panels' and 'Even with an array rated above 400W, the S2000 cannot accept more than that limit.' Arithmetic: two PS200 in parallel = 48 V / 8.32 A, inside the 28-60 V window; in series = 96 V, above the 60 V top of the window. The blog itself only says to confirm that a parallel arrangement is supported.
